Image Resizer Online

Set a maximum width or height, keep the aspect ratio, and optionally pick a target file size. Advanced settings are open on this page.

Compression tool

Target size Target size:
Advanced settings

By default the tool keeps quality reasonable (about 62% or higher) and reduces dimensions to reach small targets; tick “Keep dimensions” to prefer full size at lower quality. Aspect ratio is always preserved and images are never enlarged. PNG is lossless and may not reach a small target; JPEG/WebP are lossy. JPEG replaces transparency with white; WebP and PNG keep it.

Resize and compress together

Enter a maximum width and/or height. The image is never enlarged. The tool then compresses to the chosen KB target.

Why resizing helps file size

Halving width and height removes about three quarters of the pixels, which usually cuts file size far more than quality changes alone.

Resize by pixels, then compress by KB

A resizer changes the number of pixels in a picture. File size follows pixel count closely: halving both width and height leaves about a quarter of the pixels. This page combines the two ideas. You choose a maximum width and height, and the tool also fits the result to a target file size.

Leave both boxes empty to keep the original dimensions. The tool never enlarges an image, so a larger maximum than the original has no effect.

Common resize sizes

Typical needs include small profile pictures, thumbnails for listings, images for documents and slides, and exact portal requirements. Check the destination's required size and enter it. Because the aspect ratio is preserved, if you set both width and height the picture fits inside that box rather than being stretched.

This tool does not crop or stretch to an exact width and height. If you need an exact shape, crop first in a photo editor.

Why resizing often beats lowering quality

Reducing quality strongly produces visible blocks. Reducing dimensions keeps each remaining pixel clean. When a picture will be viewed small anyway, extra pixels are simply wasted bytes. The tool downsizes in steps for a sharper result.

Step by step

Open Advanced settings, enter a maximum width (and height if needed), pick a target size, add the file, and review the result card. If the image is still above the target, lower the maximum width further or choose JPEG or WebP.

Examples

Resize a 4,000 by 3,000 pixel photo to a maximum width of 1,200, and it becomes about 1,200 by 900. Resize a tall portrait with a maximum height of 800 and it fits inside that height. Set a target of 200KB and the tool compresses the resized picture to fit.

Resize for web, email and documents

For a web page, match the largest displayed size. For email, widths around 1,000 to 1,600 pixels are usually enough for viewing. For documents and slides, consider the page width. Keep the original file for printing or later edits.

Limits

Only JPEG, PNG and WebP are supported. Files above 50 MB or 50 megapixels are rejected. The tool does not rotate, crop or stretch images, and it does not edit metadata.

Resizing and file size together

When you set both a maximum size in pixels and a target in KB, the tool applies the pixel limit first and then searches for the best quality or additional reduction that meets the KB target. This is useful for portals that specify both. Check the final dimensions on the result card, because if the target is difficult the tool may reduce the picture below your maximum to reach it, and it tells you when it does.

Resizing screenshots

Screenshots are often very wide because of high-density displays. Reducing a 2,880-pixel-wide screenshot to 1,440 pixels removes about three quarters of the pixels while usually remaining readable. Use PNG or WebP for text-heavy screenshots and compare the preview before downloading.

Common questions

Does the resizer enlarge images?

No. Dimensions are only reduced, never increased.
